lessons.title: Regime Persistence vs Regime Noise: How Long Do Regimes Actually Last?

body.text: A genuine regime persists. A single bad day, a single good day, or a single stock's earnings surprise does not. The entire discipline of regime detection comes down to telling these two things apart, fast enough to matter and slow enough to not be fooled.

children.text: So far this chapter has treated regimes as if they are obvious once you know to look for them: a calm uptrend, a panic selloff, a choppy range. In practice the hardest part is not naming a regime after the fact. It is deciding, on the day something unusual happens, whether you are looking at the start of a new regime or at noise inside the old one. This lesson gives you a way to reason about that question using persistence, before Chapter 2 turns it into concrete detection rules.
Not Every Wiggle Is a New Regime

Nifty can fall 3% in a single session on a global cue, an RBI surprise, or a single heavyweight stock's earnings miss dragging the index, and fully recover within a week with realized volatility back to where it started. That is noise: a real move, but one that does not persist or spread across the trend, volatility, and correlation dimensions together. A genuine regime shift shows up in more than one dimension at once and keeps showing up for weeks, not days.

columns.label: Genuine Regime Shift
points: Shows up across trend, volatility, and correlation together, not just one dimension
Persists across multiple confirmation windows (weeks), not a single session
Usually traceable to a structural cause: a rate cycle, a policy shift, a systemic shock
Realized volatility resets to a new, sustained level rather than snapping back

columns.label: Noise / False Signal
points: Shows up in one dimension only, often just a single day's return
Reverts within days as the move that caused it fades
Usually traceable to an isolated event: one stock, one headline, a thin-volume session
Realized volatility spikes for a day or two, then decays back to its prior level

children.text: How Long Do Regimes Actually Last?

Different regime types have very different typical lifespans, and the episodes from the previous lesson illustrate the range. Trend regimes tend to run the longest. Range-bound regimes sit in the middle. Extreme volatility regimes are usually the shortest-lived, because markets cannot sustain panic-level volatility indefinitely; either the shock resolves or participants simply run out of capacity to keep selling at that pace.

body.text: The duration ranges and the trading-day split above are rounded, illustrative estimates built to match the well-documented general shape of these regimes, not a precise classification run on tick-level NSE data. Chapter 2 builds the actual measurement tools.

children.text: Extreme volatility regimes are rare in trading-day terms but account for a wildly disproportionate share of drawdowns and of realized profit and loss for a systematic book. This is exactly why they cannot be ignored just because they are a small slice of the pie above.
A Simple Way to Think About Persistence

There is a clean way to connect 'how long does a regime last' to 'how likely is it to still be the same regime tomorrow.' If a regime has a constant probability p of persisting from one period to the next, its expected duration follows directly from the geometric distribution.

body.caption: Expected regime duration, where p is the probability of remaining in the same regime from one period to the next

children.text: If a regime has a 90% chance of persisting from one week to the next, its expected duration is 1 / (1 - 0.90), or 10 weeks. Drop that persistence probability to 60%, and the expected duration falls to 2.5 weeks. Small changes in p produce large changes in how long a regime is expected to last, which is exactly why estimating p carefully matters far more than it first appears to.

stats.label: Volatility Spike, Illustrative Weekly Persistence

body.text: This persistence probability, p, is not just a convenient shortcut. It is the exact quantity a Hidden Markov Model estimates as a self-transition probability, the probability of staying in the same hidden state from one period to the next. Chapter 3 shows you how to estimate it properly from data instead of assuming it.

children.text: Why This Tension Shapes Every Detection Method You Build

Every detection method in this course sits somewhere on a line between two failure modes. React to every single-day move and you get a system that flags a new regime every time noise hits, whipsawing itself the same way the crossover system in Lesson 1 whipsawed on false trend signals, except now the whipsaw is in your regime labels instead of your trade signals. Require weeks of confirmation before declaring a regime shift and you get a system that is technically accurate but arrives so late it has already missed most of the move it was supposed to catch. Chapter 2 starts with simple rules that sit closer to the fast, noisy end of that line. Chapter 3's Hidden Markov Model sits closer to the slower, statistically disciplined end. Chapter 7 measures exactly how much that lag costs in a realistic backtest.

body.text: There is no persistence threshold that eliminates this tradeoff. Every choice of confirmation window trades false positives for lag. The goal in the chapters ahead is not to find the setting with zero cost, it is to choose the tradeoff deliberately instead of by accident.

body.title: From Persistence Probability to Expected Duration
body.prompt: A volatility regime has a 65% probability of persisting from one week to the next. Using E[duration] = 1 / (1 - p), what is its expected duration in weeks?
body.explanation: E[duration] = 1 / (1 - 0.65) = 1 / 0.35 ≈ 2.86 weeks. A 65% weekly persistence probability implies this volatility regime is expected to last under three weeks before flipping to another state, well short of a typical trend regime's expected duration at the persistence probabilities shown in this lesson.

body.title: Naming the Quantity
body.textWithBlank: The expected duration of a regime equals 1 divided by (1 minus its ___ probability), the chance it remains the same regime from one period to the next.
body.explanation: This is the self-transition probability, later formalized in Chapter 3 as a diagonal entry of a Hidden Markov Model's transition matrix. The higher it is, the longer a regime is expected to persist before switching.

children.text: That closes the intuition-building half of this course. You now have a working definition of a regime across three dimensions, three real Indian market episodes to test that definition against, and a framework for telling a genuine shift from noise. Chapter 2 turns all of it into measurable, computable rules, starting with the simplest ones a systematic desk actually uses.

points: A genuine regime shift shows up across trend, volatility, and correlation together and persists for weeks; noise shows up in one dimension and reverts within days
Trend regimes tend to last the longest, range-bound regimes sit in the middle, and extreme volatility regimes are typically the shortest-lived
Extreme volatility regimes are a small share of trading days but account for a disproportionate share of drawdowns, so their rarity does not make them safe to ignore
Expected regime duration equals 1 / (1 - p), where p is the probability of remaining in the same regime from one period to the next
This persistence probability p is the same quantity Chapter 3 formalizes as a Hidden Markov Model's self-transition probability
Every regime detector trades false positives for lag; there is no setting that removes this tradeoff, only a deliberate choice of where to sit on it
